First off, I'll have to give you a little more background on what Feynman diagrams really are. Basically, they operate on the principle of "Anything can happen, but some events are more likely than others." And every event that could happen needs to adhere to a certain set of principles (conservation of energy, conservation of momentum, and a bunch of other conservation principles and symmetry rules I won't get into). The diagrams are a way to keep track of all of that. And the more requirements (every point where lines meet, called a vertex, has a bunch of these) means the interaction is less likely to occur. So the more vertices in the diagram, the more esoteric the event.

One possible event that can happen is this one where a photon comes from the left, spontaneously decays into a virtual electron and anti-electron, which then recombine to a photon which carries on as if nothing happened. You'd think it wouldn't matter, but it does. When two photons undergo this same event near each other, those virtual electron-positron pairs can start interacting with each other. And that's where this box diagram comes from. The photons cannot interact with each other directly, but they can briefly decay into electron-positron pairs, which can then influence and annihilate with each other and create two slightly different photons.

TL;DR: Photons don't interact directly with each other, but they can interact and decay into electrons/positrons, which can in turn influence other photons. This almost never happens.
